steps.text: Credential dumping looks confirmed, so I'm checking the user and host identifiers involved—user-4dfd9c5b8a and the host tied to that runs_process relationship rel-5f3a0682d3. I'll pull that host entity to verify the source.

arguments.reasoning: Find host entity id running rundll32.

steps.text: I could also check the parent process of powershell, but just checking for the process alone should be sufficient.

I've confirmed this alert is malicious: a PowerShell session launched rundll32 using the comsvcs.dll MiniDump trick to dump LSASS memory into a Temp folder, a clear credential-theft technique. I recommend isolating workstation5, preserving and deleting the dump file, rotating affected credentials, and investigating the originating PowerShell session.

submission.reasoning: On workstation5 at 2020-10-18T23:50:05Z, an interactive powershell.exe (PID 6100) spawned rundll32.exe (PID 4824, High integrity, WORKSTATION5\wardog) running 'comsvcs.dll MiniDump 756 C:\Users\wardog\AppData\Local\Temp\lsass-comsvcs.dmp full', a living-off-the-land technique. rundll32 opened lsass.exe (0x1410, then 0x1FFFFF). The call trace for the full-access open runs through comsvcs.dll and dbgcore.DLL (the minidump library), and the process wrote lsass-comsvcs.dmp to the user's Temp folder. This is confirmed LSASS credential dumping (T1003.001). Not checked: what started PowerShell and whether the dump was taken off the host. Response: isolate the host, delete the dump (keep a forensic copy first), rotate wardog and every credential cached on the host, and investigate the parent PowerShell session.
